speaker: Philippe Laffont
title: He Turned  Million Into a Nearly  Billion Investment Firm | Philippe Laffont
question: In technology investing, how can an investor recognize a genuinely foundational shift early rather than mistaking a routine product cycle for a new era?
guest: I was a very good historian of technology. I got in my mind this view, from 1750 on, of all the different technologies and how they diffuse and go up and back down. From 1750 to 1950, you had two hundred years of the Industrial Revolution. In 1950, we moved from the industrial age to the information age with the first semiconductor and mainframe. From 1950 to 2020, we had seven waves within that seventy-year block: the mainframe, minicomputer, PC, networking, internet, mobile internet, and cloud—each wave about ten years. Then we get a new semiconductor piece that leads to a gigantic new age, the intelligence age. The atomic unit of the intelligence age is the GPU, like a neuron, and all those fiber-optic cables connecting GPUs together are the synapses. We've moved from calculator-style semiconductors that you just make smaller and faster to a brand-new architecture that mimics the brain. You have to recognize when you stumble onto a wave versus when you stumble onto an age—an age is comprised of multiple waves, and this is the third fundamental shift in how society produces and gets organized.

points.core: Studying long-run technology history reveals recurring patterns in how new innovations diffuse.
points.note: Accept: historical analogies across industrial and computing eras, studying past technology adoption curves and displacement cycles. Do not credit: generic advice to do thorough research or follow industry news.

points.core: Investors must distinguish decade-long platform waves from rarer multi-wave technological ages.

points.note: Accept: shifting from faster/smaller sequential chips to networked parallel GPUs or brain-like transformer architectures, changing the atomic unit of compute. Do not credit: generic mentions of disruptive innovation or AI hype.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A foundational shift usually shows up as a collapse in the cost of something basic, such as computing, bandwidth, storage, or intelligence, by an order of magnitude or more, rather than as a better version of an existing product. That cost collapse makes previously uneconomic activities viable, so the clearest early signal is new behavior and new kinds of companies, not just faster upgrades of old ones.

Several other markers help. Developers and talent migrate to the new platform before revenue does. Complementary layers form around it: tools, infrastructure, and standards that others build on. Adoption is driven by genuine pull from users, often starting with uses that look like toys, rather than by vendor marketing. Incumbents find it awkward to respond because the shift undermines their business model, not just their product. And improvement keeps compounding along a steep curve rather than flattening after one release.

A routine product cycle, by contrast, leaves industry structure, profit pools, and user habits intact.

Two cautions: real shifts typically take longer than expected and still produce bubbles, so being right about the technology does not guarantee being right about valuations or winners.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: A routine product cycle makes existing workflows faster or cheaper within established unit economics, whereas a foundational shift collapses the marginal cost of a core constraint—such as compute, distribution, or cognition—making previously impossible behaviors economically trivial. Early on, investors can spot this difference not in polished enterprise roadmaps, but in unscripted builder and user pull. Genuine platform shifts often look like clumsy, underpowered toys to incumbents, yet they attract obsessive developers and organic, unsubsidized usage despite rough edges, spawning unexpected applications rather than neat feature upgrades. Instead of slotting into existing workflows, a foundational technology demands native architectures and reorganizes how value is captured across the stack. The sharpest litmus test is incumbent tension: if market leaders can bolt the innovation onto their current products to reinforce existing margins, it is likely a routine cycle; if embracing it fully requires cannibalizing their pricing model, customer relationships, or distribution moat, a new era has begun.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A real foundational shift changes the cost structure of an activity, not just how good the product is. Look for a drop of 10x or more in the cost of something basic, like computing, storage, bandwidth, or now cognition, and for that drop to keep compounding. A routine product cycle makes existing products better. A platform shift makes new behaviors and business models possible that weren't economical before.

There are several useful signals. Developers and tinkerers adopt it before big companies do. People use it heavily even when the early product is crude, as with the early web and smartphones, rather than buying it once and drifting away. Complementary businesses start forming around it, such as tooling, infrastructure and new startups. Incumbents brush it off as a toy because it doesn't serve their best customers yet, which is Clayton Christensen's pattern. Finally, look for second-order effects: whether it reshapes distribution, labor or customer expectations across many industries rather than one.

Be skeptical when the main evidence is hype, funding announcements or demos with little repeat use. Use your judgment about adoption curves and unit economics, not stories. Remember too that being right about the era doesn't guarantee being right about which companies win it, or how long it takes.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: A genuinely foundational shift rarely announces itself through polished features; instead, it reveals itself by collapsing the cost of a core capability by an order of magnitude, making previously uneconomic workflows suddenly viable. While a routine product cycle improves an existing experience on a predictable upgrade cadence, a true platform shift forces users and businesses to reorganize how they operate. Early investors can spot the difference by watching where technical talent and startups concentrate. When builders create native products that only work on the new paradigm—rather than incumbents bolting new features onto legacy tools—the shift is likely structural. Another telltale sign is durable organic pull despite rough early interfaces: if users tolerate friction because the underlying utility is irreplaceable, demand is real rather than promotional. Finally, look at incumbent hesitation. Routine cycles reinforce market leaders, whereas foundational eras threaten their business models, creating a window where new architectures and value chains can quietly take root.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Look for a change in what’s economically possible. A foundational shift makes an important activity cheap enough, fast enough, or accessible enough that people start doing things they previously couldn’t justify. A routine product cycle mostly gives existing buyers a better way to do what they already do.

Early evidence comes from behavior. Are customers redesigning workflows, moving recurring budgets, or using the technology more as costs fall? Are independent developers and businesses building around it? Look for repeated use and spending across unrelated customers. Launch demos and pilot counts tell you less about whether the change will stick.

Then ask who gets paid as adoption grows. A technology can reshape an industry while competition drives down profits for its pioneers. Before investing, write down what you expect to see next, such as repeat purchases or falling deployment costs, and what evidence would make you change your mind.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Look for a change in what people can afford to do, how often they can do it, and who can do it. A routine upgrade gives existing customers a reason to buy again. A foundational shift also makes previously impractical activities viable. Cloud computing, for example, let a small team launch a service and add capacity as demand grew, without buying servers in advance.

Early on, look for independent teams using the technology to solve problems its creators never anticipated. Then follow their customers. Do they keep using it once incentives expire? Does usage deepen as the price falls or reliability improves? Those signals carry more weight than launch sales or a polished demo.

Make the thesis testable. Name a use case that should become economical at a specific cost or performance threshold, then track adoption once the technology crosses it. Even if the shift is real, ask separately which company can capture the value and how much success its share price already assumes.
